comments.author: PsychonautAlpha
comments.body:
Based on my experience creating pixel art by hand and working with AI for my day job, I would wager that a lot of it is for the same reasons that it is difficult to give a 2D image to a model and get a truly good "first pass" 3D model of the same thing as output.

There are simply a lot of layers of abstraction that the model has to read through to make the kinds of determinations that it must to get a good "first pass", and most models just aren't built for it. 

In the case of pixel art, each pixel carries SO much weight, often times representing multiple abstract things that the human eye/brain can infer, but a model cannot. A single pixel might represent an iris, the entire eye, a shadow that is being cast over the cheekbone, and a contour line that gives form and volume to the entire head of the sprite all at once, and it might also suggest something about the orientation of the figure, whether it is a 3/4 turn to the left or right, and it might also be a marker of the artist's style.

One pixel.

And when taking a 2D image and trying to infer a 3D model, a human often has to make some determinations about where shadow ends and volume starts, which shapes are foreground and which are background, and where adjustments need to be made to render 2D shapes as plausible 3D space. LLMs typically aren't equipped to evaluate meaning in that kind of way, so they do the best that they can based on description input.

I'm not 100% positive on all of this, and I'm not an AI researcher, but I've worked with it enough to understand what kinds of inputs the heavy LLMs are good at and what they struggle with, and this seems to be the case for a lot of it.

comments.author: Betrome
comments.body:
Yeah, I've been trying to get a workflow going for my game Farroad, and I think I'm just now starting to work out the kinks. I started by training a skill regarding the aesthetic I was going for, as well as specific rules like color limits and proportions.

I use Qwen for generation, and had to do a lot of trial and error to find a good prompt. I use that over a wide range of seeds to narrow down and eventually find a generation I like. Then Claude realizes it from 1024x1024 to 228x128 and conducts a pass to clean up colors and pixels and clean the background with BiRefNet. It then shades sections of the body different shades to prepare for animation.

From there I use Wan 2.2 video to create rough animations that are then run through keyrestore to rebuild each frame independently following the rules I mentioned above. I have custom Python scripts such as bob.py that adds subtle single pixel movement and rigrun.py that adds a rig specifically for running animations. After getting sla good motion it re colors the animation too much the master sprite.

Finally, it draws a grid over each frame for more specific edits. I give it the coordinates and the edits that needs made and it makes them, which generally takes 1-3 steps. 

After that it exports the animations directly to Godot. I use Opus 5.5. lower models couldn't do it effectively.

comments.author: because-potato
comments.body:
I have a really convoluted pipeline with codex and pixel lab. Took me weeks to make, but I can share the agent with you if you want. 

I basically have chat gpt generate a base image of what I want, feed it to codex, codex converts to a 256x256 sheet, puts that into pixel lab, generates animations, then uses python to clean up the animations. 

So far I have north/south/east/west animations for idle, walking, walking equipped, idle equipped, damage recoil, attacking, attacking unarmed, and have male/female versions of all those sprites. 

I also have an engine for clothing where I just draw onto a clothing template, and the engine automatically wraps the clothing onto all those animations. It also supports eye color variation, and I’m working on 4 direction hairstyles.

I feel like I’m reinventing the wheel for sure but it works, and it requires very little supervision at this point. 

If I want a shirt, I describe it to ChatGPT, it makes 10-20 options based on my description, I pick the one I like, feed it to codex, and in 10 minutes I have a craftable shirt that can be wrapped onto all of my animations. 

My pixel art style is similar to stardew valley, probably about 30% more details.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
There ARE, but the models are specialized and expensive. Pixel Lab and Sprite Fusion are the most reliable. 

  
Pixel art is an extreme extension of the old strawberry problem for next-token prediction. For something as small as a sprite, how do you tokenize it? Like, let's say you want to build a LoRA for pixel art, and you want to plug that LoRA into a local model. How are you going to train that LoRA? You could take ripped sprite sheets and start feeding them in, but that's not going to accomplish anything unless you can successfully caption the data. 

In pixel art, how do you define what a leg or an arm or a face looks like? These are incredibly abstracted and varied because you're working at such a small scale. And that LoRA has to be able to successfully associate whatever you want to conceptualize as a pixel art arm with the larger model's understanding of what an arm is.

  
A LLM that was highly specialized and dedicated to just one style probably would work well enough, because it would be that much easier to tokenize the data. I'm confident that a model grown from the ground up to replicate Metal Slug art by digesting well-captioned ripped assets could do so. 

But who is going to do that? It would be insanity. That audience for that capability would be incredibly small, the liability would be incredibly high, and the cost of making the machine would be ludicrous.
